cards.title: The Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant η∈(0,1/2), is there a rational constant δ∈(0,1/2) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with δn an integer, distinguish YES: some S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≤η, from NO: every S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≥1−η.
cards.why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs G=([n],E), n≥2 and d≥1, given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty S, ∂_G S is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and Φ_G(S)=|∂_G S|/(d|S|). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants η,δ are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For δ=a/b in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since η<1/2; inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each x∈L to a YES graph and each x∉L to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on η and its chosen δ. The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every η by choosing δ and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed η. Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed δ at that η would refute the hardness claim under P≠NP; an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly Φ_G(S). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If δ=1/1000, the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

sentences: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size?
The target set occupies a fixed fraction δ of the graph, with δ chosen after the gap parameter η.
Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set.
A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size.
Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
